title: Chapter IX

teacherSummary.text: Tormented by guilt, Victor considers suicide. His family withdraws to Belrive. Victor journeys into the Alps toward Chamounix, where the majesty of mountains, glaciers and Mont Blanc offers temporary relief.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Nothing is more painful to the human mind, than, after the feelings have been worked up by a quick succession of events, the dead…” slowly and put it in my own words: Victor says nothing hurts the mind more than the dead calm of inaction and certainty after a rush of events. Next, craft. I notice the contrast between "quick succession" and "dead calmness," which turns stillness into torment. The strongest word is “calmness”: it is normally peaceful, but here it is "dead," the calm of guilt with nothing left to do. Then, effect. Why is the calm after the trial so painful for Victor? My answer: The calm after the trial is so painful for Victor because William and Justine are dead and he can neither undo nor confess; the stillness leaves him alone with his responsibility.
